body_markdown:
There are a litany of exciting moments in the progression of a project car from a junky hulk to a functional and attractive vehicle. Oftentimes, the project requires an amount of work that feels like a mountain, and when complete we are just happy to finally be done. Yet we are not done, and those who have traversed this path before know torquing the last bolt is merely the start of the rollercoaster that is enjoying your project. There will be loops, and you may spend a bit of time inverted on this ride, but there are some things we can do to help get the car on the road more quickly and make it more reliable, which is what we all want, right?


The amount of time a project car spends up on jackstands often directly correlates to the our willingness to be patient and ease into enjoying the now “complete” car. The lure of a first drive is intoxicating, and I’m not here to take away that thrill from anyone. Do the first drive. Revel in the excitement. Then start sorting the car. Congrats, you’ve now entered the part of a project that people point to when discussing how projects never technically end. This is the time to do meaningful inspections and take stock of what is working as expected—and what might still need some fine tuning or re-thinking. Here are a few shortcuts that get you to the fun driving a little faster.


## Ease Into It


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


With freshly built or otherwise untested things like recently revived barn finds, it’s best to ease into driving so both the car and you can get feeling for what is normal or strange, without the pressure of being too far from home or getting stuck in a high-consequence environment like traffic. Think of the place you work on or store the car as a the center of a bullseye laid on a map, with each concentric ring representing a boundary for driving the car. Keeping close to home keeps consequences relatively low and also helps ensure we take short trips and are forced to stop and inspect regularly.


Once you feel comfortable and are having no trouble with shorter trips, head across town or take routes with more traffic. This essentially lets you limit testing to one new thing. First drives on straight, smooth roads near the house to ensure the drivetrain works as expected, before increasing range to include roads with corners and traffic to bring in the brakes and steering, without the distraction of thinking about the engine and transmission at the same time. Any drive in a car is often a stew comprised of a lot of things, but isolating and tasting each piece individually when working on a new recipe ensures we don’t miss things, or worse, misdiagnose and end up chasing our tails.


## Short, No-Pressure Road Trip


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The increasing radius works for awhile, but at some point there comes a time to break free and stretch the new build’s legs, while likely cramping yours. That’s right: road trip. Nothing crazy, but enough to really make all the parts of the car really work. If you don’t ever plan to drive more than an hour from home in you car, this drive should be at least that. Personally, I like to do an hour away from home and an hour back. That’s often enough time that both the car and I can settle in and get an honest picture about usability, comfort, and economy.


Make this trip a fun one, but also no-pressure. That means there isn’t a show or vacation at the end, there’s no deadline. Stack the deck in your favor. Have four hours marked aside for a one-hour drive. Then, even if it turns into 45 minutes of driving and three hours of roadside repair and getting the car back home, you are actually 15 minutes early… Things will pop up. This is when they should pop up, so plan the time to deal with them right away, and then it’s done.


## Phase the Build


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Hearing this LS run before dropping it in place ought to be a treat.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Ready to wrestle it back into place.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Just like the testing radius above, allow for focusing on individual systems. It’s also possible to achieve a similar helping effect by returning the car to driving condition between projects. For[this Corvette build](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/project-corvette/) , I opted to get the car driving first in order to find what absolutely needed attention and to confirm it was a good starting point for the idea I had. Only then did I swap the engine and transmission, which got the car back to driving shape so I could lightly sort it out, before I took to pulling the differential to swap final-drive ratios. This allowed me to hear and understand the noises and feel of the new engine and transmission, which meant I could divorce those from my mind when testing the differential. This is especially helpful with vibrations or other situations where the last thing you touched is often the problem. But if you last touched five different parts of the car, well, have fun with diagnostics.


## Leave a Fuse


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


If you are making changes or “improvements,” more than likely you have altered the expected durability of at least a few components. Unless you want first drives to be a regular recurrence, leaving a known fuse is wise to prevent your hard work from going up in smoke. For me, that is the tire choice on my overpowered Corvette. While it’s more tire than what the factory fitted in 1985, I still have less grip—both in contact patch size and tire compound makeup—than this drivetrain combination wants. That is nice for helping get to know the car and its new character, without wondering what the first thing to break will be—because I know I don’t have enough traction to break things further up the drivetrain.


Soon enough, I’ll put more time, parts, and work into this car, but for now I get to enjoy driving the Corvette truly anxiety-free, because I tested this project and it passed. At least, for what I want out of this build right now, which is a fun car to drive around town and with friends. Expectations will change in the future, as will parts and systems, and thus the sorting process will be run though again. And again. It’s all part of project-car fun, though.
